**2026-09-20 — SLICE 45 (memo slice 2): `authorizePortal()` + the deny matrix — AND THE CONTACT-WRITABLE CENSUS WAS A SPECIFICATION THE SCHEMA DID NOT IMPLEMENT.** `src/portal/` now holds the contact plane's authorization seam: the frozen capability table and the two profile bundles (`capabilities.ts`), the pure verdicts (`policy.ts`), the module-gate reader (`module-gates.ts`), `authorizePortal()` + `withPortalRead()` (`authorize.ts`) and `requirePortalContext()` (`context.ts`). No UI, no projection, no route — as the memo's slice order says. **THE FINDING OF THE SLICE, and it is the one the memo said this slice exists to produce.** TENANCY.md §7.2/§11, SECURITY.md §7 and AUTHZ.md §8 all state the same closed set of contact-writable rows. **The database did not.** Measured, not suspected: `tenant_isolation` is PERMISSIVE **FOR ALL** on every class-B table and `portal_gate`'s WITH CHECK only pinned the row to the contact's own client, so a contact principal could INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE `client`, `contact`, `project`, `project_version`, `milestone`, `service`, `document`, `project_time_summary` and `time_report`, and could DELETE any CLIENT_VISIBLE `work_item` / `work_item_activity` — those two deny INSERT and UPDATE through `portal_gate`'s WITH CHECK, but **a DELETE is decided by USING, and USING is the READ gate**. The sharpest was `contact`: a **self-signup and a self-promotion to `CONTACT_PRIMARY`** at the data layer, against the invariant slice 1 closed three separate ways on the AUTH path — `disableSignUp`, the `portalAuthClient` refusal and the absent INSERT policy all defend the auth plane, and **none of them is in force inside an ordinary contact transaction**; `contact_auth_path_immutable` does not cover it either, because that trigger keys on `app.auth_contact_id`, which only `src/db/portal-identity.ts` sets. None of it was reachable — no application code has ever handed a contact-principal transaction to a write — and that is exactly why it had to be closed BEFORE the slices that start handing contacts real surfaces. Migration `20260920230000`: three named RESTRICTIVE policies per class-B table (`portal_no_insert` / `portal_no_update` / `portal_no_delete`), named rather than folded into `portal_gate`'s qual so that opening one is a visible `DROP POLICY` a reviewer meets, not a two-character edit inside a boolean.

**AND THE FIRST CUT OF THAT MIGRATION BROKE THE ONE WRITE IT EXISTS TO PROTECT — caught by the POSITIVE CONTROL and by nothing else.** `portal_no_update` was written as a USING deny, the shape `comment` has carried since 2W. The census's positive control then failed: a contact could no longer insert a comment at all, `COMMENT_SUBJECT_GONE`. The subject was there — measured under one principal, in one transaction: `SELECT id FROM work_item WHERE id = $1` returned one row; the same statement with `FOR SHARE` returned **zero**. **Postgres applies the UPDATE policies to a row LOCK**, so a RESTRICTIVE `FOR UPDATE … USING` deny makes every row of that table unlockable by a contact, which reads to `comment_denorm_guard` (which takes `FOR SHARE` on its subject since the write-skew fix) as "the subject does not exist". Nothing structural could have seen it: the policy set was exactly as designed, the census pin passed, and every denial test passed HARDER than before. Migration `20260920233000` makes `portal_no_update` a **WITH CHECK** deny with no USING — the lock consults the (now absent) USING, the write still fails the WITH CHECK — applied uniformly rather than only to the tables a contact path locks today (`work_item` via the comment guard, `document` via its DOCUMENT and FILE_VERSION branches), because that list grows and a per-table rule is one that gets got wrong. `portal_no_delete` stays a USING deny: DELETE has no WITH CHECK and a row lock consults UPDATE policies only. **A deny-matrix without a positive control measures whether the database is reachable at all.** It cost a second migration because the first was already applied; the second carries the whole explanation, which is the better place for it anyway.

**THE SECOND FINDING, and it fails OPEN in three directions at once.** `requireAccess()` resolves gates 1–3 inside the caller's transaction. Doing the same under a contact principal is not slower or cheaper — it is silently WRONG: `feature_flag`, `tenant_preference` and `tenant` all carry `portal_deny`, so a contact-principal read of each returns ZERO ROWS, and zero rows means *enabled* to every existing reader (`flagEnabled` treats a missing flag as on — correctly, flags gate rollouts; `parseEntitlements(undefined)` falls back to the everything-on default; `preferenceEnabled` treats a missing row as enabled). Gates 1, 2 and 3 would all have passed for every tenant, **including a tenant that had deliberately switched the portal off**, and no test running inside a contact transaction could have caught it: the answer is identical to the correct one whenever nothing is switched off. So `resolvePortalModuleGates(tenantId)` runs in its own short transaction under the **system** principal, once per request, memoised by `requirePortalContext`. That does not bend "portal reads never run under a system principal" — that rule is about PROJECTIONS ("a projection built under `system` has lost the RLS net") — and the safety argument is structural rather than promised: the return value is a fixed-shape map from a compile-time module list to one of four enum states, with no row, no id and no database string anywhere in it. Both halves are measured in one dbtest: the gates resolve correctly AND the same three reads under the contact principal return `{preferences: 0, tenants: 0, flags: 0}`.

**THREE DELIBERATE READINGS, stated so a reviewer can disagree with them rather than discover them.** (1) **The pipeline runs in §8's order, not §5's** — module gates LAST. The gates are AND-ed so the outcome is identical; the order fixes only the REASON, and on this plane §8's order is better: a contact who is not allowed anyway never learns whether their agency's plan includes invoicing. (2) **"was invited" is enforced on the ROW.** §8's gloss makes invite-only a property of the codebase ("no self-signup path exists in code"); `authorizePortal()` additionally requires `Contact.invitedAt` to be stamped, so an activation path that forgets to record the invitation is refused rather than trusted. **Anything that activates a contact must set `invitedAt`** — the invite slice owns that. (3) **The continuity exemption is read wider than §5's letter:** the three `portal.continuity.*` capabilities skip gates 2 and 3 for the `portal` module as well as for `continuity_box`, because a lapsed subscription lapses both keys at once and a promise that survives one key but not the other is not a promise. Gate 1 (the engineering kill-switch) and the profile gate still apply. Phase 8 confirms this against CONTINUITY_BOX.md.

**SMALLER, BUT WORTH THE INK.** *(a)* `authorizePortal()` re-reads `portalStatus` and `portalProfile` from the `contact` row inside the transaction instead of trusting the session — a member who suspends a contact or demotes it expects that to bite now, not at the next sign-in; both directions are pinned by a dbtest that changes the row mid-flight. *(b)* `portal.report.view` is in AUTHZ's table marked v2 and is deliberately **absent from the union in code**, because `CONTACT_PRIMARY` is derived as "every capability" — listing one early grants it early. The derivation is a convenience; the exact-list pin in `capabilities.test.ts` is the control that makes it safe. *(c)* Steps 3–4 (resource ownership + visibility + `portalEnabled`) are ONE row read under the contact principal, not a comparison: comparing `project.clientId` in TypeScript would need the row first, and getting the row means passing the very gate the comparison was meant to make. "No row" means `NOT_FOUND`, indistinguishable from a nonexistent id. *(d)* **Column-level GRANTs do work here and the first migration's header understates it** — `notification` already carries `GRANT UPDATE (read_at, archived_at, snoozed_till)`. A column grant cannot say "a contact may write only these columns while a member writes others" (both are `app_runtime`), so a per-principal column rule still needs a trigger; but where NO principal may write the rest, the grant is the right tool and the approval-column slices should reach for it first. Corrected in migration `20260920233000`'s header, the only place it could be — the first migration was already applied. *(e)* The census found one doc drift: the granted column set is `read_at`, `archived_at` **and `snoozed_till`**; three documents name only the first two.

**THE ONE LOCAL FAILURE, dispositioned on evidence — and the FIRST VERSION OF THIS PARAGRAPH TAUGHT A FALSE RULE, which the code review caught.** The full local `test:db` came back **1 failed / 521 passed**: `ordering.dbtest.ts`'s 12-way concurrent-move test, `assertInScope`'s `tx.project.findFirst` dying at *"5415 ms passed"* against the 5 s budget. Precedent alone would have been enough to wave it through — the same file failed the same way on the local Neon link in slices 43 AND 44 and passed both times on the CI service container — but this slice CHANGES THE RLS POSTURE OF `project` AND `work_item`, exactly the tables that test hammers, so precedent is not evidence. Measured: re-running the file alone gave **17/17, 17/17, then 2 failed** — intermittent, not deterministic.

~~"the new policies are `cmd` ∈ {INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE} with no `ALL` and no `SELECT`, so the statement that failed (a SELECT) is provably untouched"~~ — **that reasoning is WRONG and this section is where a false rule would do the most damage.** An UPDATE policy is emphatically not irrelevant to a SELECT: a LOCKING select consults the UPDATE `USING`, which is the entire reason migration `20260920233000` exists, two paragraphs above. And `moveItem` genuinely takes `SELECT 1 FROM work_item … FOR UPDATE` (`rank-lock.ts`), so that test does lock a table this diff touched. The conclusion survives, for the reason the first version did not give: **the shipped `portal_no_update` carries no `USING` at all**, so there is nothing for a lock to consult. (Also corrected: 33 new policies plus `comment`'s two from 2W, not 35.)

**AND THE REVIEW'S OWN DIAGNOSIS OF THE FLAKE IS BETTER THAN "a slow link", so it is recorded as OWED rather than re-run away.** The test fires 12 `moveItem` transactions that serialise behind one `FOR UPDATE` on the anchor, each under the default 5 s Prisma budget whose clock starts when ITS transaction opens — so the twelfth must absorb eleven predecessors' round trips before it does any work of its own. That is a structural property of the test against a fixed budget, not a defect that CI green disproves, and it will resurface on any slower link (it has now cost three slices an investigation). The durable fix is a widened `timeoutMs` for that one test, or fewer movers — **`ordering.dbtest.ts` belongs to 2W and is deliberately not touched by this slice; the next session that opens that file should do it.**

**THE TWO FRESH REVIEWS — code + security, read-only, given the diff and the gate results and nothing else. Neither saw the implementing reasoning.** Security **cleared all seven areas it was asked for on traced evidence**, with no CRITICAL and no HIGH: cross-client/cross-tenant (it checked something I had not — `src/auth/portal.ts` configures no `cookieCache`, so Better Auth re-reads the `contact` row per request and the session's tenancy cannot be stale or forged); the policy set is exactly `B_clientScoped ∪ B_projectScoped` minus `comment`; privilege escalation closed at the policy AND the trigger level; the module-gate fail-open argument verified claim by claim; the seam rules; and the NOT_FOUND indistinguishability, including that all four out-of-scope outcomes take the same single query so there is no timing separation. **But both reviews landed independently on the same objection, and it was the right one: the slice MEASURED three holes, pinned them as allowed, and justified them with reasons that do not survive checking — on the very standard the first migration set for itself.** Migration `20260921000000` closes them.

**TAKEN (10).** *(1)* **`search_index` DELETE was never needed and was left open for no reason.** The claim "narrowing it would break that path" is true for INSERT and UPDATE (`search_upsert` is `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`) and FALSE for DELETE: `search_feed_comment`'s delete branch fires only on a comment DELETE or soft-delete, neither of which a contact can perform. What it cost: `portal_gate` on `search_index` binds client, visibility and portal_enabled and **nothing else**, so a contact-principal `DELETE … WHERE client_id = <own>` would have silently emptied the TENANT'S OWN STAFF SEARCH of every client-visible row. *(2)* Same policy bound no `entity_type`, so a contact could plant rows of any type (the `project_id IS NULL` branch needs no project) or rewrite the `title`/`body_text` members read; INSERT/UPDATE are now pinned to `entity_type = 'COMMENT'`, the exact width of the path. *(3)* **`audit_event` let a contact forge a MEMBER'S audit row.** `audit_tenant_insert` pinned the tenant and nothing else, `audit_portal_select_deny` is SELECT-only, and `audit_event_immutable` makes every row permanent — write-only evidence poisoning in the one table SECURITY.md §7 treats as evidentiary. Now: under a contact principal an insert must describe the contact itself (`actor_type='CONTACT'`, `actor_id = app.principal_id`, `visibility='TENANT'`), which is exactly what `audit.record()` already produces there, so the legitimate future path is permitted verbatim and nothing else is. *(4)* **`comment` gives up the last `USING`-shaped deny.** Leaving it was defensible today and both reviewers verified that no contact-caused path locks a comment — but it left the dangerous shape on the ONE table a contact writes, against the previous migration's own argument that a per-table rule is one that will be got wrong. *(5)* **The sealed-box exemption never checked whether the box was sealed.** §5 conditions it explicitly — "**once a box is SEALED**" — and the code applied it unconditionally, so a tenant that never bought `continuity_box` passed gate 2 anyway: the commercial gate on continuity was not enforced for contacts *at any time*. It now takes `continuityBoxSealed`, default **false**, so Phase 8 cannot forget the precondition and the capabilities are gated normally until someone proves it. *(6)* **And it was too wide in the other direction:** the first cut waived gate 3 for the `portal` module too, so a tenant that deliberately switched the portal off would still have served continuity to contacts — the exact failure `module-gates.ts` exists to prevent, reintroduced for three capabilities. Gate 3 is now waived only for `continuity_box`, which is what §5 words. *(7)* **`resolvePortalModuleGates` failed OPEN on a missing tenant row** — `parseEntitlements(undefined)` is the everything-on default, so `tenant?.entitlements` on a null row resolved every gate to "ok", reproducing "absent means enabled" **inside the function whose forty-line header refuses to accept it from the contact principal**. One line, and a dbtest that asks for a tenant that does not exist. *(8)* **`portal-writes.ts` escaped the forbidden-columns grep.** The founder's split exists so that "this code runs as system" is a property of a filename — and `portal-projections.test.ts` matched the name `portal.ts` exactly, so the split made that file more dangerous and less watched at once. Mutation-checked with a probe file: with the old walk a `portal-writes.ts` containing `assigneeMemberId` passes silently; with the fix it fails. *(9)* **The step-0 guard validated the ambient context, not the `tx`.** A system `tx` captured in an outer scope and used inside a `withPortalRead` callback satisfied it while every read ran as `system`. `withPortalRead` now STAMPS the handle it hands out (a `WeakSet`) and step 0 refuses any handle it did not stamp — exact, at the cost of a lookup rather than a round trip. *(10)* The census had a false NEGATIVE for a table with RLS never enabled (no `pg_policies` rows ⇒ skipped as "nobody may do it"); it now reads `relrowsecurity`/`relforcerowsecurity` and is self-sufficient for raw-SQL tables like `search_index`.

**ALSO TAKEN, smaller:** the contact row is memoised PER TRANSACTION (a projection checking three capabilities paid three round trips on the plane that can least afford them; per-transaction keeps the mid-session-suspension semantics exactly); `PortalScopeRef`'s docstring no longer implies coverage it lacks (two kinds today — every other resource kind is owed by the slice that introduces it); the `Notification` row of TENANCY §7.2's table now names `snoozed_till`.

**DISPOSITIONED, NOT TAKEN (2).** *(a)* **`gates` is caller-supplied data on `PortalPrincipal` and could be spoofed all-"ok" by a route that builds its own principal.** True — and the member plane has the identical shape for the identical reason: `MemberActor.mfa` is caller-supplied, and AUTHZ.md §7.5 answers it with a rule ("only `requireTenantContext()` should build actors for ✦ paths") rather than a mechanism. Branding the type does not close it (a spread survives branding), and resolving the gates inside `authorizePortal` puts a system-principal round trip on every capability check. The type's doc comment now carries the same sentence its member twin does. Revisit only if the member plane's does. *(b)* ~~**Test tenant slugs are not `e2e-` prefixed.**~~ — **TAKEN AFTER ALL, and the "convention nit" was pointing at a real registration step.** The reviewer was right that something was off and wrong about which direction: `e2e-` is the prefix the BROWSER harness SWEEPS BY AGE, so a dbtest adopting it would have its fixtures deleted mid-run by a concurrent e2e run. What a dbtest owes instead is a per-suite prefix **registered in `DBTEST_PREFIXES`** (`e2e/fixtures/seed-cli.ts`), which is what lets `sweep-dbtests` collect its orphans — and I had not registered either of mine. Regenerating that list with the two greps its own comment documents turned up **six** unregistered prefixes, four of them PRE-EXISTING (`desc-`, `portalc-`, `switch-*`, `tree-`), whose orphans no sweep had ever collected — the same failure the file's comment already records having happened once ("missed sixteen real ones, so a sweep would have reported success"). **And the recipe itself has a blind spot:** both greps look for a `slug:` key, so a fixture passing a shorthand `{ slug }` property is invisible to them, which is exactly how `pauthz-` escaped on the day it was written. All six registered; the recipe's comment now names the shorthand trap; `portal-authz.dbtest.ts` spells its literals out; and its two tenants were renamed `pauthz-a-`/`pauthz-b-` because `pauthz2-` does not start with `pauthz-` and would have orphaned on a near-miss prefix. **AGENTS.md's rule is corrected** (founder decision, 2026-09-20): it said throwaway tenants are `e2e-` prefixed, which is true only of the browser harness and actively wrong for a dbtest.

~~The original disposition:~~ AGENTS.md says throwaway tenants are `e2e-` prefixed — but `e2e-` is the prefix the BROWSER harness SWEEPS (tenants older than its 90-minute age guard), so a dbtest adopting it would expose its own fixture to deletion by a concurrent e2e run. The whole dbtest corpus uses its own prefixes (`scope-`, `projects-`, `gate-`) for that reason. **Left as is, and flagged as a documentation mismatch for the founder:** AGENTS.md's sentence should say "a throwaway tenant your own test provisions and tears down", with `e2e-` named as the browser harness's prefix specifically.

**WHAT SLICE 3 INHERITS.** *(Slice 3 landed 2026-09-21 — see the top of this section. (1) is closed for every AUTHORIZATION denial and deliberately not for admission; (5) is taken. (2), (3) and (4) stand: (3) is now a locked shell at `/portal/login` rather than a missing route, and the portal plane still writes no audit rows.)* (1) **Denial reasons are internal.** `authorizePortal()` throws `AuthzError` with a precise reason for the audit row, the log and the test matrix; the portal's HTTP surface must render every one of them identically — a contact told `NOT_ENTITLED` has been told something about their agency's commercial arrangements. The first route owns that. (2) **The portal plane still writes NO audit rows** (slice 1's owed item, unchanged) — and `authorizePortal()` denials are not audited either. Both must land with, or before, the first path that can activate a contact. (3) `/portal/login` is still a `PUBLIC_PATH` with no page behind it. (4) `src/authz/portal-projections.test.ts`'s walk matches any file named `portal.ts`, which already includes `src/auth/portal.ts` and would include a future `src/portal/portal.ts`; `src/portal/`'s files are deliberately named otherwise. (5) The `contact` row is readable by any contact of the same client (`portal_gate` there is structural, client-match only), so it carries `invitedById` — a MEMBER id — into a contact's reach. RLS grants the row; the projection owns the columns. Slice 3's forbidden-columns list should consider `invitedById`.

**2026-09-20 — PHASE 3 HAS STARTED. SLICE 44 (memo slice 1): the contact identity stack, and the pinned design for it could not have worked as written.** The portal Better Auth instance, its three AUTH-class tables, the admission gate and both proxy arms have landed. **PUSHED AND GREEN: `73d9f5d`; CI run [35529323966](https://github.com/azcheema/fortleva/actions/runs/35529323966) — BOTH JOBS `success`.** Unit **1125 passed / 1 skipped**; `test:db` **39 files / 493 passed, 0 failed** (the two `ordering.dbtest.ts` concurrency tests that failed on the local Neon link pass on the service container, exactly as the stashed control predicted — a ~37 ms link against a 5 s budget, not a defect); browser harness **132 passed, no flaky**. The new files run green in CI too: `portal-identity.dbtest.ts` 24, `portal.dbtest.ts` 11. **THE FINDING OF THE SLICE, and it is the kind the memo predicted.** DATA_MODEL.md §6.4 pins the portal instance as "modelName-mapped user→Contact". `contact` is a class-B TENANT-SCOPED table whose `tenant_isolation` policy is `tenant_id = app.tenant_id` — and **sign-in has no tenant, because the tenant is what an email lookup is FOR**. With the GUC unset that comparison is NULL, so the mapped instance reads ZERO rows and no contact could ever have signed in. The member plane never meets this: its `user` table is global with a blanket `allow_runtime USING (true)`. Three ways out existed and only one survives the rules already written down — a global `ContactIdentity` table re-litigates a settled pin, and a `withPlatform` shim puts a BYPASSRLS connection behind an UNAUTHENTICATED endpoint, which is the worst trade in the product. So: the **`withUser()` shape** (migration `20260808200000`, the "my tenants" lookup), which solves the identical problem on the member plane — a transaction-local GUC naming the one row the request already supplied, and a policy that admits that row and nothing else. `contact_auth_lookup` keys on `app.auth_contact_email` OR `app.auth_contact_id`, set only by `src/db/portal-identity.ts`, the FIFTH narrow entry point (pinned to one importer by an ESLint belt AND `import-boundary.test.ts`, like `recordPlatformEvent`).

**THE ADMISSION IS READ-ONLY, AND THAT WAS NOT THE FIRST DESIGN — the database refused the first one and was right to.** The first cut added a matching UPDATE policy. Every auth-path update then died on `42501 new row violates row-level security policy for table "search_index"`: `contact` carries an AFTER trigger feeding the search index, whose own RLS wants a tenant nobody has yet. **Making that pass would have meant widening the search index to an unauthenticated plane** — far worse than the problem. So auth-path WRITES are brokered through `withTenant(tenantId, {type:'system'})` in the tenancy the lookup just proved, exactly as AUTHZ.md §8 already requires for every contact-caused write, and the migration was rolled back and re-applied without the UPDATE policy. Two consequences worth keeping: **invite-only is now a DATABASE fact** (no INSERT policy ⇒ even a signup endpoint mounted by accident is refused by RLS — three independent noes with `disableSignUp` and the delegate), and because a system transaction may write any column of its tenant, the brokered write carries `app.auth_contact_id` INTO that transaction so the `contact_auth_path_immutable` trigger stays live: **tenancy, client, portalProfile and portalStatus cannot be changed by anything the auth plane caused.**

**TWO DOCUMENTED CONTROLS THAT DID NOT EXIST — one corrected, one BUILT after the security review showed it was load-bearing.** SECURITY.md §3.3 described the portal instance as having its "own secret" and the contact session as carrying `plane = CONTACT`. Neither was true: `ContactSession` has no `plane` column at all, and all three instances shared one `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` while better-call signs the cookie VALUE and **not its name**. The `plane` half is simply corrected — the TABLE is the audience. The *secret* half turned out to matter more than documentation hygiene: the review traced that Better Auth's email-verification artifacts are **self-contained JWTs carrying no plane claim**, so the table barrier — which protects sessions — does not protect them at all, and `/verify-email` mints a session before any password is checked. The portal instance now derives its **own secret** (`portalAuthSecret`, from the shared one, so there is nothing new to provision and nothing existing to invalidate), which makes every portal-signed artifact structurally unverifiable on the other two planes and vice versa, with no hook to remember on any instance. A member token pasted under `__Host-flv.portal` therefore verifies its signature perfectly — and resolves to nothing, because the **TABLE** is the barrier. That is the ops-plane lesson `src/proxy.ts` already carries, and it is now measured in both directions rather than asserted (`portal.dbtest.ts`, "the planes do not leak into each other"). A third: DATA_MODEL's `ContactVerification` listing omitted `updatedAt`, which Better Auth's core `verification` schema gives a `defaultValue` and therefore writes on EVERY create — the first invite token would have died on an unknown-argument error. Corrected at the model.

**AND THE ONE I GOT WRONG BY READING THE SOURCE — the repo's own standing lesson, collected again.** I concluded from `@better-auth/prisma-adapter`'s `getJoinKeyName()` that the `Contact` relation field MUST be named `contactaccounts` (model name, lowercased whole, plus "s") or sign-in would die on an unknown include field, and wrote that into the schema as a do-not-tidy warning. **A mutation check passed with the field renamed**, which meant the claim was false. A probe recording the adapter's actual calls showed why: native joins are used only under `experimental.joins`, which this product does not set, so the factory fetches the relation with a SEPARATE query and no include key is ever built. The only two calls it makes on this model are `findFirst {where:{email:{equals}}}` and my own hook's `findFirst {where:{id},select:{portalStatus}}`. The names are ours; they are readable again, and the comment now records the measurement instead of the inference. **Two review verifiers were disproved by a browser on cmdk; here the source disproved itself under a mutation. Measure.**

**GATES AND EVIDENCE.** Unit **70 files / 1119 passed / 1 skipped** (+2 files, +28 — `portal-gate.test.ts` and `portal-identity-policy.test.ts`, both database-free by construction: the pure policy lives in its own importless module for the reason `platform-gate.ts` does, since the unit suite runs before `migrate deploy` with no `DATABASE_URL`). New dbtests: `portal-identity.dbtest.ts` (22) and `portal.dbtest.ts` (9). **Four mutation checks, because a passing test is not evidence until it has been made to fail:** drop `tenantId` from the instance's `additionalFields` ⇒ the session-fields test fails; make the admission hook accept any status ⇒ both admission tests fail; add a blanket `USING (true)` SELECT policy to `contact` ⇒ **five** RLS tests fail, the cross-tenant one included; remove `auth/portal.ts` from the boundary allowlist ⇒ the scan names it. **A NEAR-MISS WORTH THE SAME WEIGHT AS A FINDING:** the first ESLint belt was written as a new config block listing only its own concern — and ESLint flat config gives the LAST matching block the rule OUTRIGHT rather than merging, so it **silently switched the raw-client restriction off across the tree**. It surfaced only as a handful of "unused eslint-disable" warnings in `src/auth`, which is exactly how it would have shipped. The blocks now compose from named shared constants, and four probe files verify the belt bites on `@/db`, on the module path, and inside `src/jobs/**` — while the raw-client rule still fires.

**THE TWO FRESH REVIEWS FOUND THE SAME HIGH, AND IT WAS A HOLE IN THE SLICE'S CENTRAL CLAIM.** Both agents got the diff and the gate results and nothing else. **The invite-only invariant was enforced three ways for the `contact` ROW and zero ways for its CREDENTIAL.** Better Auth's `/reset-password` calls `createAccount` when no credential exists, and merely CONFIGURING `sendResetPassword` mounts the unauthenticated `/request-password-reset` that issues the token — so a contact a member had only *recorded* (`NO_ACCESS`, never invited) could have set themselves a portal password, with no invitation, no single-use token, no expiry and no audit row, which would have become a live login the day anyone activated them. Closed at the database (`contact_account_requires_invite`: a credential may exist only for an INVITED or ACTIVE contact) plus a refusal to MAIL a non-ACTIVE contact — declining inside `sendResetPassword` rather than short-circuiting the endpoint, because its response is deliberately constant and turning that into a 4xx would make it an account-enumeration oracle for every agency's client list. **Proven both ways:** an end-to-end test drives the real endpoints, and with the trigger disabled it fails — the credential really is created. The three documents that asserted "nothing creates a `ContactAccount`" are corrected in place.

**SIX MORE REAL ONES, and three were my comments asserting something false.** (a) **`update` did not intersect its `where` with the admitted id** — only `updateMany` did, justified by a comment claiming Prisma's unique `where` names one row. It does not: `WhereUniqueInput` takes `AND`/`OR` alongside the unique field and the adapter emits exactly that. Both branches intersect now. (b) Three places asserted the `42501 search_index` failure in the PRESENT tense; it belongs to the rolled-back first design, and with the shipped policies a tenant-less update dies on `contact` as a P2025 instead — **and the dbtest named for that claim set `app.tenant_id` and asserted the update SUCCEEDED**, measuring nothing. Rewritten to assert the P2025 by code. (c) The admission refusal was byte-distinguishable from a wrong password (own message, no `code`) beside a comment saying the two were indistinguishable; it now reuses the library's shape and a test compares it against a REAL wrong-password body so the hand-copied constant cannot drift. (d) **Belt two's portal scan missed `import * as db from "@/db"`** — the namespace grab its platform sibling has always caught, and precisely what belt two exists for, since five files in `src/auth` carry a file-level `eslint-disable` that switches belt one off. (e) The auth-path read used Prisma's untuned 5 s budget instead of the product's `txOptions()`, on the one transaction a user cannot retry around. (f) `contact_auth_lookup` compared against the empty string, which would admit any row whose email really is empty; `nullif(…,'')` closes it structurally and the test now inserts such a row instead of relying on none existing.

**AND ONE GATE GOT STRONGER THAN THE SLICE NEEDED.** The posture dbtest asserted class-B policies with `toContain`, so it could not see an ADDED one — and PERMISSIVE policies OR together, which makes a stray `USING (true)` the worst mistake this schema can make. It now asserts the exact PERMISSIVE set per class-B table (RESTRICTIVE additions can only narrow, so they stay free), with `contact_auth_lookup` declared. Mutation-checked: a blanket policy on `contact` now fails it.

**WHAT IS OWED, stated so the next slice does not have to rediscover it.** (1) **The portal plane writes NO audit rows** — both other instances carry an `AuthAuditSink` and this one carries none, so `auth.login_succeeded`/`auth.login_failed` do not fire for a contact, and neither do the brokered auth-path writes to `contact`. Still deferred, and the safety is measured rather than assumed: **no contact can sign in today**, because nothing in application code ever writes `portalStatus` away from `NO_ACCESS` (only tests do). It must land with, or before, the first path that can activate a contact. (2) `/portal/login` is now a `PUBLIC_PATH` and the redirect target, but **the page does not exist yet** — a contact with an expired cookie currently gets a 404 instead of the member sign-in form they used to get, which is the better of the two wrongs. (3) `/portal/invite/*` will need the same public treatment when the invite flow lands; it is deliberately not pre-added. (4) **`/verify-email` on the portal 500s and cannot work**, because Better Auth's `updateUserByEmail` keys on email and the seam only updates by id. It fails CLOSED and nothing needs it — invite acceptance will set `emailVerified` on the tenant path — but do not "fix" it by allowing email-keyed writes without re-reading why the portal has its own `secret`. (5) `/request-password-reset`, `/reset-password` and `/send-verification-email` are now in `RATE_LIMITED_PATHS` for all three planes. The earlier note here named `/forget-password`, **which does not exist in better-auth 1.6.26** — a key matching nothing reads as coverage and is worse than an absent one.

**FOUNDER DECISIONS 2026-09-20 (four questions asked with recommendations, all four taken) — PHASE 3 IS UNBLOCKED, AND IT STILL STARTS IN A NEW SESSION.** The load-bearing questions in `docs/research/2026-09-20-phase-3-decision-memo.md` §4 are answered. §3's slice order stands as written (memo Q3, not re-asked), and so does the memo's own advice on model and effort: **Opus 5 at high throughout, and `/security-review` on EVERY Phase 3 slice regardless of what the diff appears to touch** — the `/members` gap in slice 41 was found by a reviewer reading what a single grep hit actually was, and that is the class of finding Phase 3 will produce most of. The four answers, so the next session does not re-ask them:
1. **View-as-Contact runs under the MEMBER'S OWN SESSION** (memo §2.1, option 1). The contact projections are called with a SYNTHESISED contact principal; there is no second cookie jar, the pins' "reuses the exact same functions (asserted by import graph)" assertion still holds, and the stale-tab fence (slice 29) stays a non-issue rather than becoming a design problem. 4. **"Only mentions" stays a dead setting until Phase 3 closes it.** No migration. This settles the "OPEN, AND THE FOUNDER'S TO ANSWER" note below.

**THE REVIEWS OF SLICE 43 — TWO FRESH READ-ONLY AGENTS (code + security), 18 findings, and the sharpest one was aimed at this slice's own evidence file.** Both agents got the diff, the gate results and nothing else; neither saw the implementing reasoning. **SECURITY CLEARED ALL SIX AREAS IT WAS ASKED FOR, on traced evidence rather than on my comments** — the added GUC is transaction-local (`is_local = true`, so it cannot survive a PgBouncer handoff), parameter-bound so not injectable, and fails closed because it shares a statement with the four tenant GUCs; `AuthzError` (no `.code`), `DomainError` (closed union) and an RLS refusal (zero rows ⇒ P2025) can none of them satisfy `isLockTimeout`, so no denial can be dressed up as contention; the migration needs no grants, and the one real index/RLS interaction (a non-leakproof operator evaluating ahead of a RESTRICTIVE policy) does not apply to btree equality on uuid/text. **THE PARTIAL-FAN-OUT QUESTION WAS SETTLED THE RIGHT WAY** — by reading the trigger, not the prose: it is a plain `AFTER UPDATE … FOR EACH ROW`, not a `CONSTRAINT TRIGGER`, and the function body has **no `BEGIN … EXCEPTION` block**, which is the only construct that would open a subtransaction and let leg 7 fail while legs 1–6 stayed applied. A starved switch therefore rolls back all ten legs and the project row; the portal cannot be half-open in either direction.

**TAKEN (10).** *(1)* **The HIGH, and it was mine in the worst place:** `portal-contention.dbtest.ts` — the file that IS the measurement of record — repeated the very sentence the slice exists to refute ("the wait ran to the whole transaction budget and arrived as a P2028"). PLAN claimed "every copy of the false sentence is corrected in place" while the slice was creating a new one. Rewritten to state the measurement. *(2)* `withTenant` no longer PINS `lock_timeout = '0'` for callers that did not ask; it emits the setting only when a bound is requested. The first cut sent '0' everywhere on the grounds that 0 is the server default — true today, checked in `pg_settings` — but it would have silently defeated a later `ALTER ROLE app_runtime SET lock_timeout = '10s'`, the textbook hardening against exactly this hang, in the one seam all tenant work passes through, with no test able to see it. *(3)* `retryOnContention` retried two shapes and `setPortalEnabled` translated ONE: a deadlock surviving three attempts went up raw and reached the member as a 500 on the emergency control. Both shapes now map to `PORTAL_SWITCH_BUSY`, each with a detail breadcrumb that never reaches the UI. *(4)* `retry.ts` contradicted itself inside one diff — "TWO CALLERS" beside "its three callers"; two is right and the argument that rested on three is rewritten. `DEADLOCK_ATTEMPTS` → `CONTENTION_ATTEMPTS`. *(5)* **`PORTAL_FANOUT_LEGS` is no longer a hand-counted 10.** Neither reviewer found this; looking for a home for their point, `PORTAL_ENABLED_FANOUT_TARGETS` in the model registry turned out to be the list `isolation.dbtest.ts` already checks the trigger body against, so the budget now derives from it — `+ 1` for `search_index`, the one leg no TypeScript list can name because it is deliberately not a Prisma model. A new projectScoped model widens the budget in the commit that gives it a leg. *(6)* PLAN's ordered item 2 and §2.3 of the **Phase 3 memo** both still said the exposure was open AND said it was a P2028 — in the two documents the next session is directed to read first. Both corrected; the memo keeps the wrong text underneath, marked, because the error is instructive. *(7)* The migration comment named seven legs and claimed eight (`time_report` was missing) and said nothing about `CREATE INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY` — in a migration whose whole subject is lock windows. Both fixed; CONCURRENTLY cannot be used at all, since Prisma wraps each migration in a transaction. *(8)* The dbtest compared LINK_FACTOR-scaled measurements to unscaled constants; the redundant ceiling is gone and the holder's timeout is a flat generous one. *(9)+(10)* Unit pins for `isLockTimeout` and `retryOnContention` — the sibling predicate carries nine tests precisely because it was wrong twice, and the new one had none; its dangerous direction is a FALSE POSITIVE, a real error read as contention and reported to the member as "try again".

**THE TEST GAP THAT TOOK TWO GOES, and it is the lesson of the review.** The code reviewer pointed out that **setting the attempt count to 1 left every dbtest passing** — nothing anywhere proved a blocked switch RECOVERS, which is the retry's entire purpose. A recovery test was added, releasing the blocker after 1.3 bounds… and the mutation check showed it **still passed at one attempt**. The arithmetic was wrong: the lock wait does not start until `requireAccess` and `loadInScope` have made their round trips, so writing S for that setup, attempt k spans [S + (k−1)·bound, S + k·bound]. "An attempt definitely failed first" needs release > S + bound, which at 1.3 bounds demanded S < 0.3·bound — and S over the Neon link sits right on that line. At TWO bounds both conditions hold for every S in [0, bound), with no assumption about link speed. Re-mutated: at one attempt the recovery test now FAILS, at three it passes. **A test written to close a gap is not evidence until the mutation check says it closes it.**

**DISPOSITIONED, NOT TAKEN (1) — and both reviewers found it independently, so it is recorded in full.** The budget derivation `LEGS × BOUND` is **not a worst case**. `lock_timeout` is spent per lock ACQUISITION, and an acquisition is per contended ROW, so one leg can wait its full bound once per row a different transaction holds. Several distinct concurrent holders on one project can therefore exceed `PORTAL_TX_MS`, and `lock_timeout` is structurally incapable of bounding that — only `statement_timeout` (57014) cancels a statement on its total time. What happens then is a P2028, untranslated, which the member meets as a 500 on a control that nonetheless rolled back cleanly. **Left deliberately visible rather than dressed up as contention**, because a fan-out that genuinely takes 25 s is a bug someone should see, and because the motivating case — a bulk edit — is exactly one holder per leg. The claims are corrected everywhere ("the member is TOLD" now says *against one holder per leg*; "comes back in seconds" now says *typically ~4.5 s, bounded by attempts × the transaction budget*). `statement_timeout` is the tool if that case ever stops being hypothetical.

**REJECTED (1), because the reviewer miscounted.** The code review called `rank-lock.ts`'s "the other eight tables have no queue at all" wrong. It is right: ten legs, minus `work_item` (the one leg joining the work queue would cover) and minus `milestone` (which queues on its own `milestone_rank:` key), leaves exactly eight with no queue. Left as written. *(The standing lesson applies in both directions — a review finding is a claim to check, not a verdict to apply.)*

**2026-09-20 — SLICE 43: the portal off-switch can no longer be starved — and the reason it could be was NOT the one three files stated.** Slice 40 left this open and the Phase 3 memo (§2.3) promoted it from a footnote to a risk: turning a project's portal OFF is the emergency "stop showing this client our data" control, a bulk edit holding `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` makes the ten-table fan-out BLOCK rather than cycle, and no deadlock retry ever matched it. **THE CORRECTION, AND IT IS THE FINDING OF THE SLICE.** `service.ts`, `rank-lock.ts` and §0 all said that unbounded wait "dies as P2028 at `withTenant`'s 5 s budget". It does not. Measured, by removing the bound and shrinking the transaction budget to **3 s** with a row lock held against it: **the call was still waiting past 30 s.** Prisma's interactive-transaction timeout is enforced around the queries the client ISSUES, not inside one the database has PARKED on a lock — and nothing else bounded it either, read out of `pg_settings` on the real datasource rather than assumed: `lock_timeout` 0 and `statement_timeout` 0, both `source = 'default'` with nothing set on the database or on `app_runtime`, and the single bound that IS configured (`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, 5 min) catches a transaction sitting IDLE, never one actively waiting on a lock. The real pre-slice behaviour of this control was not a 5 s failure but a request that hung until something upstream gave up, holding every lock the fan-out had already taken for all of it. Every copy of the false sentence is corrected in place. **WHAT SHIPPED.** (i) `withTenant` takes `lockTimeoutMs`, set transaction-locally beside the existing GUCs (`set_config(…, true)`; '0' — Postgres's own default — for every caller that does not ask, so nothing else changes). (ii) `isLockTimeout` (55P03) beside `isDeadlock`, and `retryOnContention` beside `retryOnDeadlock` in `src/lib/retry.ts` — SEPARATE exports sharing one loop, because a lock timeout can only reach a caller that asked for the bound and a future caller should not inherit a retry it never reasoned about. (iii) `setPortalEnabled` passes both budgets, DERIVED from each other rather than picked: `lock_timeout` is spent per LOCK WAIT and the trigger runs ten UPDATEs, so a single attempt's worst case is every leg waiting its full bound and the transaction budget must exceed that (`PORTAL_FANOUT_LEGS * PORTAL_LOCK_WAIT_MS + 10s` = 25 s, the legs now derived from the model registry rather than counted by hand) or the thing that fires first is the failure the bound exists to replace. (iv) When the attempts are spent — on EITHER retried shape, after the review caught only one of them being translated — the member is TOLD, `PORTAL_SWITCH_BUSY`, en + sv, instead of shown a 500; nothing was written, so "try again" is the whole truth. (Against one holder per leg: see the dispositioned finding above for the case the bound cannot cover.) The `Switch` is controlled from the server prop and `useRun` already toasts `ok:false`, so the failure never looked like a revert and no UI change was needed. **WHY NOT SIMPLY WAIT IT OUT:** a switch that hangs for a minute and then either worked or did not is worse than one that comes back in seconds and says which — and while it waits it holds locks that make everything else on the project slower, which is the opposite of what an emergency control should do. The OFF direction gets no longer allowance than ON for that reason. **AND THE FAN-OUT ITSELF WAS SLOWER THAN IT HAD TO BE — migration `20260920190000`, DDL only, no smoke run owed.** Eight of the ten legs have an index whose PREFIX is exactly `(tenant_id, project_id)`. **Two did not:** `work_item_activity`, whose three indexes are all `(tenant_id, work_item_id, …)` or `(tenant_id, client_id, visibility)` — so the best the planner had was the `tenant_id` prefix, a scan of the TENANT'S WHOLE ACTIVITY HISTORY to find one project's rows, on the fastest-growing table in the product — and `service`, the same defect with far fewer rows. A leg that scans is a leg that holds its locks longer, so the widest window for this contention was one the function was opening itself. Both are ALSO unindexed foreign keys (`work_item_activity`'s is ON DELETE CASCADE, `service`'s ON DELETE RESTRICT), stated as a second, smaller benefit and not as the justification: nothing in the app ever deletes a project. **THE TEST IS THE POINT.** `src/projects/portal-contention.dbtest.ts` provokes a REAL 55P03 through a real blocked fan-out on a second connection, which is what makes `isLockTimeout` trustworthy — the deadlock test next door was written from Prisma's source and had to be corrected twice (P2039 vs P2010, slice 37). **Two mutation checks, each failing where intended:** emptying `LOCK_TIMEOUT_CODES` printed the arriving error verbatim — `PrismaClientKnownRequestError`, `code: "P2039"`, at 2247 ms, so the model-call branch is MEASURED (P2010 stays by symmetry and is marked in the comment as unproven, because nothing in the product yet waits on a lock from a `$queryRaw` under a bound); removing `lockTimeoutMs` is what produced the 30 s correction above. The index assertion is deliberately STRUCTURAL (leading columns and their order, from `pg_index`) and not an `EXPLAIN` — a plan on a fixture-sized table reports the row count, not the schema. **STILL OPEN AND UNCHANGED:** the two deadlock cycles `rank-lock.ts` documents. This was the blocking shape, not the cycles.

**2026-09-20 — SLICE 42 (the founder's pick from the four recorded leftovers): `copyWeek` retries a deadlock, and a review found a SECOND writer nobody had listed.** `rank-lock.ts` has named copyWeek since slice 7 as a locker outside the work queue — every entry it writes takes FOR KEY SHARE on its item through the foreign key in DATE order, while a board drag goes by RANK — but until now only the OTHER side recovered: `ordering.ts` has retried since 2026-09-19 and nothing under `src/modules/time` tested for a deadlock at all. A copy chosen as the victim came back a 500 with the week uncopied, which is the more expensive half of that pair to lose (a drag is one row; a copy is a week of them). **THE REVIEW'S FIND:** `repriceRateCard` is a second multi-row `time_entry` writer and the hazard list had never named it. It reads by `startedAt` but WRITES one `updateMany` per distinct resulting snapshot, so its lock order is the GROUPING's, not the read's — two reprices of different cards over overlapping entries group differently and can take the same rows in opposite orders. Nothing on either side recovered. It takes the same retry, and the lesson is recorded where it belongs: that list names the lockers someone thought to look for. **WHY RETRY AND NOT THE QUEUE** for copyWeek: one copy can span several projects, so joining `lockProjectRanks` means every touched project's lock in sorted order — or a new cycle among concurrent copies — held for the length of the copy. A real contention change on a weekly path against a race never observed. `retryOnDeadlock` now has three callers, which is why it lives in `src/lib`. Verified that `guarded` does not swallow a 40P01: `mapDbError` rethrows anything no token matches and none of the time module's eleven tokens appears in a deadlock message. Gates: typecheck, ESLint 0, unit 1081 / 1 skipped, copy + time + admin + money dbtests 57 passed.

**~~OPEN, AND THE FOUNDER'S TO ANSWER~~ — THE "Only mentions" HALF IS ANSWERED (2026-09-20, top of §0: it stays dead until Phase 3 closes it, no migration). (asked 2026-09-20, answers recorded):** mentions WAIT for Phase 3 and will be built whole — which leaves **"Only mentions" a dead setting** on `/settings/notifications` until then, because `comment.mentioned` is the ONLY kind that mails at that level, so choosing it means no email ever. Not done; the founder's call whether the dead option or the migration is the smaller evil. **PHASE 3: the founder asked for THE PLAN FIRST, and it is written** — `docs/research/2026-09-20-phase-3-decision-memo.md`, and the founder's next instruction is that **Phase 3 itself happens in a NEW SESSION**. The memo's headline: the DATABASE half of Phase 3 is already built and tested (the `app.principal_id` GUC, the ten-table `portal_enabled` fan-out, `portal_gate` across 7 migrations, the `RLS_CLASSES` posture test, and `portal-gate.dbtest.ts` already proving `portalEnabled=false ⇒ 0 rows`), while the APPLICATION half does not exist at all (no `ContactSession/Account/Verification`, no `authorizePortal()`, no `modules/*/portal.ts`, no `ProjectUpdate`, no portal capabilities, and `project:manage_portal` is not even in the catalogue although the pins name it). So the riskiest part is the part that is done; what is left is a second auth stack, a projection layer and ~8 screens. **FIVE QUESTIONS WAIT ON THE FOUNDER** (memo §4), the load-bearing one being the View-as-Contact SESSION model — the pins say it reuses the same projection functions but say nothing about the session, and the stale-tab fence (slice 29) exists precisely because cookies are per ORIGIN, not per tab. **AND ONE THING PHASE 3 PROMOTES FROM FOOTNOTE TO RISK:** `setPortalEnabled`'s blocking exposure (slice 40, and NOT a P2028 one — corrected and closed by slice 43, top of §0). Turning a project's portal OFF is the emergency switch, and it can fail under a bulk edit; nobody can be hurt today because nobody has a portal, but it must be fixed before the first real client logs in.

**2026-09-20 — ORDERED ITEM 4 (`comment.mentioned`) IS NOT A HAZARD AND IS NOT MINE TO BUILD. Investigated, not built, and the framing corrected — this entry IS the deliverable.** §0 has carried "`comment.mentioned` can never fire" as a standing hazard worth its own slice. It is true that nothing writes `Mention` and that the kind is catalogued (`notify/catalog.ts`, INSTANT, emails at the `MENTIONS` level — the quietest setting that still mails), templated, iconed and copied. DATA_MODEL.md says the same at the `Comment` and `Mention` models. It is a deliberate deferral with the record already straight everywhere except here, exactly like the 36 permission codes in slice 41. **AND THE REST OF IT IS PHASE 3, WHICH IS MY HARD STOP.** UI.md rule 10 spells the behaviour as "warning when mentioning/assigning a **Contact** on an INTERNAL item", `Mention.mentionedContactId` is in the schema as the XOR half of `mentionedMemberId`, and a Contact is the portal principal. The spec'd feature therefore straddles the line I am told not to cross unprompted. **WHAT IT WOULD COST, so the founder can decide without re-deriving it:** a Tiptap mention node — a NEW dependency (`@tiptap/extension-mention` + `@tiptap/suggestion`; the product pins Tiptap 3.31.3 and has neither) — plus a suggestion popup that has to survive this repo's recorded cmdk/Radix key traps, a member-search source, the server-side parse of the comment doc into `Mention` rows (minding the standing trap that ProseMirror JSON does not cross a server action unaided), the `notify.emit` fan-out, and i18n in both locales. **THE FOUNDER'S CHOICE, stated so it can be answered in one word:** a MEMBER-ONLY subset (`mentionedMemberId` alone, no contacts, no warning) is shippable before Phase 3 and is a real feature on its own; the full spec'd behaviour is not. I am not picking between them — half of a spec'd, safety-adjacent feature is a product decision, and the delegation I was given explicitly keeps Phase 3 out. **Nothing was changed in the product for this item.**

**2026-09-20 — SLICE 41 (ordered item 3): the permission audit found a REAL authorization gap, and the count it was filed under was wrong by an order of magnitude.** §0 had carried "four permission codes with no enforcement site" since the §§2W/2T audit. Audited across all 97 catalogued codes, the real number is **37** — four was a count scoped to two modules and then quoted as a total. **Thirty-six are legitimate and now say why.** Codes are immutable `resource:verb` identifiers forever (AGENTS.md), so declaring a module's set when the module is DESIGNED rather than when it ships is what stops a later slice minting a second spelling: four whole modules are waiting on features that do not exist (contracts, invoicing, reports, continuity_box), the five `issue:*` are deprecated and will never gain a site, and the rest name capabilities whose WRITE PATH is absent — `workflow:manage` (the app creates a project's default states lazily and reads them; it has never updated or deleted one), `work_item:triage`, `project_update:*`, `project_template:manage`, `billing:*`, `audit:view`, and `time:manage_locks` (the lock is REAL at the database — a locked entry refuses every edit and the time week renders a `Locked` badge — but nothing in the app writes `TimeEntry.lockedAt`; that writer is Phase 4 invoicing's, so the UI is ready for a state that cannot yet occur). **THE THIRTY-SEVENTH WAS A GAP.** `member:view`'s only occurrence in the entire product was the `permission` on its NAV ENTRY, which hides a rail link. `/members` ran on `requireTenantContext()` alone and handed the full roster and every pending invite's email to anyone who typed the URL. All four seeded templates carry `member:view`, so only a hand-built custom role could reach it, and never across tenants — RLS never wavered — but the permission existed, the rail honoured it, and the page did not. It is guarded now, shaped like `/settings/roles`: the read is refused and the page renders the forbidden state rather than 404ing, with `members.noPermission` in both locales. **HOW IT WAS FOUND MATTERS MORE THAN THAT IT WAS.** The new test did NOT catch it: its string match counted that nav entry as a guard, which is the exact false negative its own docstring admits a crude matcher cannot see. A REVIEWER reading what the single occurrence actually WAS caught it. So `nav.ts` is excluded from the scan — a nav entry is a visibility hint, never a gate — and a second review found the same hole for `dbtest-fixture.ts` and `dbtest-locks.ts`, test-only files carrying no `.test.` suffix, which a fixture granting a literal code could have laundered through. **THE AUDIT IS NOW A STANDING GATE**, `src/authz/enforcement.test.ts`, asserting an EQUALITY and not a subset, so it fails in BOTH directions: a new code with no site and no declaration fails, and so does a DECLARED code that gains one — the day invoicing ships, `invoice:issue` must leave the list and a reviewer must be asked whether its guard is in the right place. Mutation-checked in both directions before it was trusted. AUTHZ.md §3.1 carries the disposition. **One cleanup noted and not taken** (review): the inline forbidden-card shape is now in three pages and could be a shared `ForbiddenCard` — `PageState` cannot be used as-is, since beside a `PageHeader` it would render a second `h1`. Gates: typecheck, ESLint 0, unit 1081 / 1 skipped, scoping + the full visual walk 8 passed in 14.2 min. **CI run `35508076265` GREEN.**

**2026-09-20 — SLICE 40 (ordered item 2): the portal toggle retries a deadlock, and the three documented cycles are now documented CORRECTLY.** This slice changed shape twice under review and both turns are worth keeping. **THE FIRST ATTEMPT was to put `setPortalEnabled` into the work module's advisory rank queue** — the answer milestones got in slice 37. A review killed it on facts I had got wrong: the fan-out trigger is `project_portal_enabled_fanout`, not `project_stamp_portal_enabled`, and it is **TEN mass UPDATEs across ten tables** (milestone, project_version, service, document, work_item, work_item_activity, comment, search_index, project_time_summary, time_report), not one statement on `work_item`. Joining the work queue therefore covers ONE of ten legs — milestones queue on `milestone_rank:` and eight tables have no queue at all — while turning a targeted wait on genuinely conflicting rows into a project-wide wait on anything queued, and making `rank-lock.ts`'s own invariant false (no queued writer has ever locked a document or comment row; this one locks both). It also required core to import `src/modules/*`, which ARC-16 forbids and nothing in the product had ever done. **THE SECOND ATTEMPT — a deadlock retry — shipped, but its justification was wrong too, and a second review caught that as well.** I claimed the retry avoided the "emergency portal OFF loses to a bulk edit" outcome. It does not: a bulk edit holds `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` on every selected row, the fan-out's UPDATE wants the same conflicting mode, so it BLOCKS rather than cycling — no 40P01, nothing for `isDeadlock` to match, and at `withTenant`'s 5s budget it dies as **P2028**. **THAT EXPOSURE IS PRE-EXISTING AND STILL OPEN**, now named in the code and here: the portal switch can lose to a long bulk edit. The fix is a transaction budget sized for a ten-table fan-out (`withTenant`'s `timeoutMs`, which this call does not pass) and possibly a P2028 retry — both want measuring on a project with real row counts. **WHAT SHIPPED** is `retryOnDeadlock` in `src/lib/retry.ts` (four unit tests, including that it never retries a non-deadlock — the dangerous failure mode) on `setPortalEnabled`, which turns a 500 into a success for the shape a retry can answer, and costs nothing uncontended. **AND THE HAZARD NOTE IS NOW TRUE**, which was most of the value: all three cycles re-verified against the migrations rather than trusted. `document_anchor_guard` v1 reads the item with a plain SELECT and takes NOTHING — reading only that migration says the deleteItem cycle does not exist; **v2 added `FOR SHARE OF wi`** and that is the lock. `copyWeek` has NO retry of its own (nothing under `src/modules/time` tests for a deadlock), so when a copy is the victim it 500s with the week uncopied and only the other side recovers — the cheap half is `retryOnDeadlock` around its transaction, the queue is the expensive half (one copy can span several projects, so it would need every touched project's lock in sorted order). Gates: typecheck, ESLint 0, unit 1078 / 1 skipped, projects + portal-gate + documents dbtests 52 passed.

**2026-09-20 — SLICE 39 (ordered item 1): the four documents tables fit their boxes, and `KNOWN_OVERFLOW` IS NOW EMPTY.** The English ratchet has carried `files`/`client-files`/`error-banner`/`project-files` at 4-6px since slice 27 — small enough to read as rounding. **The Swedish walk is what made them worth a slice:** 14/14/14/7, the three `Filer` tables more than double, which is the first thing that instrument has paid for. **THE CAUSE was a trap this repo had already named and not finished applying:** the name cell carried a per-viewport `max-w-28 sm:max-w-64`, and a max-width on a table CELL is a FLOOR in Chromium (slice 28) — the column could not go below 112px however little room was left, while "Privat för teamet" needed 178 and the pinned actions 76. **VISIBILITY WAS NOT THE COLUMN TO CUT** even though it is the widest: it is safety-critical (UI.md §10.4), it carries all five channels of the badge, and a phone that truncated it or dropped it to a rung is the one failure this product cannot have. The name yields instead — `contain-inline-size` + `w-full` over a `min-w-20` floor. **THE SECOND HALF IS THE ONE THAT IS EASY TO MISS:** containment ALONE made the layout worse. Chromium hands spare width to the columns WITHOUT a specified one, in proportion to their max-content, and a contained cell's max-content is ZERO — so at a 1134px box the filename took 166px while the two-value badge took 370. Giving every other column an explicit width (all under their own min-content, so nothing is squeezed and the badge cannot be) makes the name the sole absorber: **101px at a 356px box, 622 at 1134, 0 scroll at every width in BOTH languages.** That is NOT the shape `/clients` uses — it declares bare heads and lets the slack spread, which works because its columns are evenly sized and cannot work here; `/projects` reaches the same end by `table-fixed`. Three tables, three answers, each measured. **Both ratchets lose their four keys in the same commit**, which is the rule: a ratchet that keeps a fixed number is a licence to regress back to it. Empty is ASSERTED, not assumed — an unlisted key is held to 0. **EIGHT REVIEW FINDINGS, and the first is a gap in the fix rather than a bug in it:** there is a FIFTH call site. The item panel renders this same table inside a peek capped at `max-w-[85vw]` — a ~298px box on a phone, under the table's own 334px minimum — so it cannot fit and still scrolls there, under the pinned column, which is the trade the pin exists for. This change improves it (366 → 334) without closing it, and **nothing measures it**, because the walk's `project-item-peek` stop shows the EMPTY attachments state: the seed attaches no document to a work item. Seeding one would put the peek under the ratchet for the first time — a slice, not something to smuggle into this one. The other seven were record-keeping in a change whose whole value is its numbers, and all were taken: local and CI figures conflated (366/11px is LOCAL, 14 and 6 are CI's); the remainder written as 102, 98 and 101 in three places; a false claim of precedent from `/clients`; `/members` undercounted at one cap when it has four; "All four keys today are bugs" left standing 30 lines under "IT IS EMPTY"; and `driftFor`'s rationale still arguing from the two keys this slice deletes. Gates: typecheck, ESLint 0, unit 1074 / 1 skipped, both width walks 8 passed in 16.7 min with the `[swedish]` log down to the backlog trade alone.

**2026-09-19 — SLICE 38: the Swedish ratchet is calibrated, from CI, and the platforms really did disagree.** Run `35443979863` (GREEN — the deadlock fix landed with it) printed the twelve `[swedish]` numbers slice 36 was built to produce, and **they are not the local ones**: `Filer` measures 14px on the runner against 11 locally, `project-files` 7 against 2, and the backlog gave 28, 29 and 30 across three local runs. A map calibrated on Windows would have been wrong on its first line — which is exactly why it landed empty, and is the clearest vindication the "calibrate from a CI log" rule has had. **WHAT THE TWELVE KEYS ARE, labelled, because `KNOWN_OVERFLOW`'s own rule says a listed number may be a TRADE rather than a bug and must say which:** eight are the settled trade — the backlog, at `lowest`'s narrow edge, **29px over a 1136px box and 27px over 1138**, one table seen four ways (plain, grouped, with a row ticked, behind the peek); the rungs were placed to make exactly this bargain, since the pinned actions column means a row's verbs never scroll. UI.md carried ~21px for this from a hand probe and the runner disagrees by 8 — the same Windows-to-ubuntu font gap this repo records everywhere else, arriving in the one figure that had never been machine-measured. **2026-09-19 — SLICE 37: CI WENT RED ON SLICE 36 AND THE FAULT WAS NOTHING SLICE 36 TOUCHED — a real concurrency defect in milestone reordering, latent since it was written.** Run `35440299558` failed `projects.dbtest.ts`'s "concurrent reorders serialise on the neighbour lock" with a Postgres DEADLOCK (40P01). Slice 36's diff is `e2e/`, `docs/` and one CI timeout — **zero `src/` files** — so it cannot have caused it; the container runner simply has more true parallelism than a developer's machine. **THE CAUSE:** `lockedRanks` was `SELECT id, rank … ORDER BY rank FOR UPDATE`, and a statement locks rows in the order it SORTS them — while `rank` is the very column a reorder UPDATES. Two concurrent movers could therefore sort the same rows differently, take the same row locks in opposite orders, and deadlock. **Two members dragging milestones in the same project at the same moment would have met it in production**, and `retryOnRankCollision` tested only for P2002, so it surfaced as a 500. The test's own name says those reorders "serialise on the neighbour lock", which is exactly what they were not doing. **THE FIX IS THE ONE THIS CODEBASE ALREADY SETTLED ON FOR WORK ITEMS AND MILESTONES NEVER GOT:** `modules/work/rank-lock.ts` (ARC-17) queues every multi-row rank writer on an advisory TRANSACTION lock, and its own header says why row locks alone are not enough — under READ COMMITTED a row lock does not refresh the statement snapshot, so two "bottom" writers can mint the same key, which is the collision `retryOnRankCollision` was papering over. Milestones now take the same kind of queue lock on their own key namespace, inside `lockedRanks` where neither caller can forget it. The locked read became a CTE ordered by `id` — immutable, so even a writer outside the queue takes the rows in the same order — and the join hands back exactly the rows the CTE locked, where a second unlocked SELECT would take its own READ COMMITTED snapshot and could return a phantom. **THREE REVIEW FINDINGS, ALL REAL, AND THE FIRST WOULD HAVE MADE THE FIX A NEAR-NO-OP:** `isDeadlock` accepted only P2010, the RAW-query shape. Traced against the installed runtime, a deadlock in any MODEL call — `tx.milestone.update`, the audit write every mutation makes — arrives as **P2039**, and once a queue lock has removed the cycle between two rank writers, a cycle through another table is exactly what is LEFT. Nine unit tests now pin all three shapes, including that a P2010 which is not a deadlock is refused. Second: `reorderMilestone` tested a STALE `m.rank` — read unlocked, before the queue lock — so a move whose neighbour had shifted during the wait could answer `changed: false` and drop silently, snapping the row back on the next read; it takes the rank from the LOCKED read now, which is `rank-lock.ts`'s own rule (re-read after every wait). Third: `rank-lock.ts` documents a live cross-table cycle for WORK items and ended "nothing retries a deadlock (40P01) yet" — true only because no predicate existed. It does now, so `ordering.ts` takes it too: a work item with a documented cycle had a weaker answer than a milestone without one. **ONE OBSERVATION WORTH AN HOUR TO THE NEXT SESSION:** `ordering.dbtest.ts` run ALONE against Neon fails its 12-way concurrency test on the 5000 ms interactive-transaction budget (5416 ms), and does so with every change here REVERTED — it is network latency, not logic, and `DB_TX_TIMEOUT_MS=20000` makes it 17/17. CI never sees it: that job runs a Postgres container on the runner. Gates: typecheck, ESLint 0, unit 1074 / 1 skipped, full `test:db` 36 files / 454 green, and ordering + projects re-run green under the wider budget.

**2026-09-19 — SLICE 36 (owed (c), and slice 17's owed (d) before it): THE HARNESS CAN SEE SWEDISH.** Swedish is this product's first locale and the wider one in almost every string a table shows, and every width this harness had ever measured was English. The gap was never theoretical — UI.md §10.12 records the backlog as ~21px over `lowest`'s narrow edge in Swedish, hand-measured with a throwaway probe, a settled TRADE that nothing could check and that therefore could not tell "as designed" from "worse than we thought" on any later change. `e2e/zz-swedish-widths.spec.ts` now switches the member's language, walks every authed stop at 390px and all nine rung widths, and measures `tableOverflow` and `offscreenRowActions`. **Its first numbers say the hand measurement was right and a little low: the backlog is 29px over a 1136px box and 27px over 1138px, 0 in English; `Filer` is 11px over a 356px box on three stops.** No screenshots and no craft audit — a contrast ratio and a row's height do not read Swedish, and those are the expensive half. **THE RATCHET LANDS EMPTY, ON PURPOSE.** Every number in it has to be CI's own: a local run measures a different app (Windows metrics against ubuntu's, 2-8px a string on this repo's own evidence), the rule in `visual.spec.ts` says re-calibrate from a CI log and never from a local run, and three local runs of this walk already gave 28, 29 and 30px for the same cell. It then took 5.1 min against a 300s budget, and the restore ran against a page Playwright had already closed, turning one timeout into two failures. And `error-boundary`'s driver clicks a button it names in ENGLISH, so in Swedish it waited the entire 600s for a control that does not exist — that stop has no table, so the walk skips `expectsFailure`, and `Stop.drive` now carries the constraint in its own doc. **SIX REVIEW FINDINGS, ALL TAKEN, and the first is the one that mattered:** the Swedish ratchet would have asserted, at zero tolerance, exactly the five stops the English walk EXEMPTS as `VOLATILE_STOPS` — and this walk runs last, so it sees more `time.spec.ts` residue than anything. `VOLATILE_STOPS` and `driftFor` moved to `e2e/fixtures/overflow.ts` and both walks share one policy. Also: the language switch sat outside the `try`, so a write that then failed its `<html lang>` poll skipped the restore — the one case it exists for; the restore could REPLACE the real failure in the report, so it is swallowed now; the "has a table" probe asked only at 1440 and would have skipped a phone-only table; `KNOWN_OVERFLOW_SV` had no name-rot guard, which now exists BEFORE the numbers do, and refuses a key on a stop that is exempt anyway; and a red Swedish walk costs 20 min with `retries: 1`, which under `timeout-minutes: 30` would CANCEL the browser job rather than fail it — raised to 40 with the arithmetic, and a note to bring it back down once the walk's real CI duration is known. Gates: typecheck, ESLint 0, unit 1065 / 1 skipped, and both walks together 8 passed in 16.7 min (the Swedish one ~4.4 of that).

**2026-09-19 — SLICE 35 (owed (d), open since slice 18): the focus reveal under the pinned column is covered — and writing the cover found a bug in the thing it covers.** The reveal exists because the browser does not see a sticky cell hide anything: a control inside the scroll box but under the pinned actions column counts as visible and is left there. **Two halves, because each catches what the other structurally cannot.** `src/lib/scroll-reveal.ts` takes the DECISION out of the handler — `revealExempt` over all five exemptions (the box, a row, a control in the pinned cell, a row with no pinned cell, focus the browser is not ringing) and `revealScrollDelta` over the geometry — and a unit test pins `revealExempt` over all 32 combinations, the shape `focusedKeyApplies` already uses. `e2e/scroll-reveal.spec.ts` then drives it in a browser, because the unit suite runs in `node`, where there is no layout at all, and so cannot say whether the component READS THE RIGHT NODES — the only bug left once the decision is pinned, and the exact class a headless browser has already disproved two source-traced conclusions about (cmdk, 2026-09-18). **THE E2E INJECTS ITS OVERFLOW, and that is a consequence of slices 28-33 rather than a shortcut:** those slices removed every table overflow the English seed produced, so the condition this behaviour needs no longer occurs on any walked stop and a test that waited for one would assert nothing. A `min-width` on the `<table>` creates the scroll and touches nothing `ScrollFade` measures. PLAN §0 named this shape — "a DOM-injected e2e at a rung edge" — before it was written. It walks a backlog row with Tab and asserts at EVERY stop rather than at one control picked in advance: never under the opaque column at any scroll position, and clear of the 32px fade as well while the table can still scroll right (at the table's end there is nowhere left to go, which is what the component always said). **THE BUG IT FOUND, on its first run:** `ScrollFade`'s ResizeObserver watched `box.firstElementChild` — which is `<Table>`'s `table-container` div, `relative w-full`, so its width IS the box's and it could never report anything new — instead of the `<table>`. The variable was even named `table`. It stayed invisible because `measure()` also runs once on `observe()`, so a table that ALREADY overflowed at first paint got its fade anyway; what went missing was later growth — a label chip added, a long title committed inline — after which content continued past the edge with nothing saying so, the other trigger being a scroll the member has no cue to perform. **THE TEST WAS MUTATION-CHECKED, which is the only way to know a new test has teeth:** pointing the pinned-cell selector at an attribute that does not exist (the "reads the wrong node" class exactly) fails it with `under the pinned column — BUTTON right 1372, column at 1364`, while every unit test stays green. **Three review findings, all taken, the first being mine to answer for:** the refactor built all five exemption inputs eagerly, which made the HOT path — the backlog's `J K`, one `focusin` per press down a four-thousand-row list — pay for two `closest()` ancestor walks it used to skip, while the comment claimed the opposite; an identity check and an `instanceof` now gate them. The spec hand-copied the fade and ring widths instead of importing them, so a shrinking `REVEAL_FADE_PX` would have left it asserting the old bound and testing nothing. And UI.md plus two PLAN lines still called this owed. Gates: typecheck, ESLint 0, unit 1065 / 1 skipped, and visual + scroll-reveal + keymap 27 passed in 17.6 min. **CI run `35437348527` GREEN.**

**2026-09-19 — SLICE 34 (owed (e)): a deactivated assignee is named, not spelled out as an id.** The backlog's assignee cell offers `activeMembers` — `status: "ACTIVE"` only — so a task held by a member who has since been deactivated sat on a value no option had, and that broke the control twice, both halves silently. `optionLabel` falls back to the raw VALUE, so the trigger's `aria-label` and `title` announced a UUID where a person's name belongs; and `NativeSelect` takes `defaultValue`, so the picker opened on its FIRST option and said **"Unassigned" over a task that is assigned**. The second half is the one nobody had written down, and it is the worse of the two. **The fix is the state cell's own current-value fallback, now a named and tested helper** — `withCurrentOption` in `src/lib/inline-edit.ts` — rather than a third copy of the idiom: the held value is prepended, labelled, and is what the select opens on; re-picking it fires no `change`, so it commits nothing. It is re-offered to NOTHING else, so a deactivated member cannot be assigned to anything new and a filtered state cannot be ENTERED, only kept. The item panel's `A` picker already reached the same end by a different road (the row is simply absent, unchecked, Enter inert) and is unchanged. **Three review findings, all taken. The sharpest was a regression the fix would have introduced:** the first draft dropped the option when the caller had no label, which for the state cell was a behaviour change from the inline code it replaced — a missing option leaves the native select anchored on some OTHER row's value, where one arrow key commits a state change nobody chose. An ugly option beats a missing one, so a nameless value is now labelled with itself; on the assignee path the case is unreachable (`assigneeName` comes from the item's own join and `User.name` is non-null, so it is null only when the id is, which is the `""` bail). A second finding retired a VACUOUS test that passed for the identity function. **ONE RESIDUAL, recorded rather than papered over:** `run()` has no optimistic assignee update, so for the second or so `router.refresh()` takes after unassigning a deactivated member, the stale row still offers her — picking her there is denied `NOT_FOUND` by `assignItem` and toasted, so it is a correct denial and never a wrong write, but it is a control offering something the server will refuse. Closing it means optimistic assignee state in the backlog, which is a slice of its own. **AND ONE GAP IN THE INSTRUMENT:** there is no e2e, because the only way to get a deactivated assignee in front of the browser is a third member in the SHARED seed, which moves the members page, the visual walk's shots and every count that reads them — a lot of blast radius for one assertion. The helper is unit-tested (five cases); the two call sites are wiring a reviewer checked. **CI run `35435342485` GREEN.**
